description: English translations of the passages in Latin, Greek and other languages than French. at: the passage in the unit (part, start, end); lang: ISO 639 code; text: the passage; translation: English; source: the author and work quoted, where the edition names them; note: a misprint or a doubtful reading. Candidates found by a character-trigram model (Latin, French, English) and Greek letters; passages fixed and translated by Claude Opus; not checked by hand.

items.text: Neque vero hoc solum natura , id est , jure gentium, &c.
items.translation: And this [is laid down] not only by nature, that is, by the law of nations, etc.
items.note: The quotation breaks off: in Cicero 'this' is the rule, laid down by the laws of peoples as well, that no one may harm another for his own advantage.

items.text: Jus naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit.
items.translation: Natural law is that which nature has taught all animals.

items.text: Quod quisque populus ipse sibi Jus constituit, id ipsius proprium civitatis est, vocaturque Jus civile , quasi jus proprium ipsius civitatis : quod vero naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit, id apud omnes peræque custoditur , vocaturque jus gentium , quasi quo jure omnes gentes utantur.
items.translation: The law that each people has established for itself is peculiar to that state and is called civil law, as being the law proper to that state; but the law that natural reason has established among all men is observed equally by all peoples and is called the law of nations, as being the law that all nations use.

items.text: Jus autem gentium omni humano generi commune est ; nam usu exigente & humanis necessitatibus , gentes humanæ jura quædam sibi constituerunt. Bella etenim orta sunt & captivitates sequutæ , servitutes , quæ sunt naturali juri contrariæ. Jure enim naturali omnes homines ab initio liberi nascebantur.
items.translation: But the law of nations is common to the whole human race; for as practice required and human needs demanded, the nations of mankind established certain laws for themselves. For wars arose, and captivity and slavery followed, which are contrary to natural law; for by natural law all men were born free from the beginning.

items.text: FECIALES, quod fidei publicæ inter populos præerant ; nam per hos fiebat, ut justum conciperetur bellum (& inde desitum) & ut fœdere fides pacis constitueretur. Ex his mittebant, antequam conciperetur, qui res repeterent: & per hos etiam nunc fit fœdus.
items.translation: Fetials [were so called] because they were in charge of the public faith between peoples; for through them it was brought about that a just war was declared (and afterwards ended), and that the faith of peace was established by treaty. Some of them were sent, before war was declared, to demand restitution; and through them even now a treaty is made.
items.note: The passage is De lingua Latina V.86 in modern numbering (the edition cites Book IV).

items.text: Rursus lex) naturalis dividi potest in naturalem hominum , quæ sola obtinuit dici lex naturæ , & naturalem civitatum , quæ dici potest lex gentium , vulgo autem jus gentium appellatur. Præcepta utriusque eadem sunt: Sed quia civitates semel institutæ induunt proprietates hominum personales , lex quam loquentes de hominum singulorum officio naturalem dicimus , applicata totis civitatibus , nationibus , sive gentibus , vocatur jus gentium.
items.translation: Again, [the law] of nature may be divided into the natural law of men, which alone has come to be called the law of nature, and the natural law of states, which may be called the law of nations (lex gentium) but is commonly called the right of nations (jus gentium). The precepts of both are the same; but because states, once instituted, take on the personal properties of men, the law that we call natural when speaking of the duty of individual men is called the right of nations when applied to whole states, nations or peoples.
items.note: The opening parenthesis of '(lex)' has dropped out in print.

items.text: Nihil est quod adhuc de Republica putem dictum , & quo possim longius progredi, nisi sit confirmatum , non modo falsum esse istud sine injuria non posse , sed hoc verissimum , sine summa justitia rempublicam regi non posse.
items.translation: I think nothing has yet been said about the commonwealth, nor anything from which I could proceed further, unless it is established not only that the claim that [a commonwealth] cannot [be governed] without injustice is false, but that this is most true: that a commonwealth cannot be governed without the highest justice.

items.text: Etenim , si hæc ( les loix ) perturbare omnia & permiscere volumus , totam vitam periculosam , insidiosam , infestamque reddemus.
items.translation: For if we are willing to throw all these [the laws] into disorder and confusion, we shall make the whole of life dangerous, full of treachery and hostile.
items.note: The parenthesis '( les loix )' is Vattel's French gloss on 'hæc', inserted into the quotation.

items.text: Qui ( principatus ) tum demum regius est , si intra modestiæ & mediocritatis fines se contineat : excessu potestatis quam imprudentes in dies augere satagunt , minuitur , penitusque corrumpitur. Nos stulti , majoris potentiæ specie decepti , dilabimur in contrarium , non satis considerantes eam demum tutam esse potentiam quæ viribus modum imponit.
items.translation: It (the principate) is truly royal only if it keeps itself within the bounds of restraint and moderation; through excess of power, which the imprudent strive to increase from day to day, it is weakened and utterly corrupted. We fools, deceived by the appearance of greater power, slide into the opposite, not considering enough that the only secure power is that which sets a limit to its own strength.

items.text: Neque enim se princeps reipublicæ & singulorum dominum arbitrabitur , quamvis assentatoribus id in aurem insusurrantibus , sed rectorem mercedem a civibus designata quam augere nisi ipsis volentibus nefas existimabit.
items.translation: For the prince will not regard himself as the master of the commonwealth and of individuals, however much flatterers may whisper it in his ear, but as its ruler, with a salary fixed by the citizens, which he will consider it a sin to increase except with their consent.
items.note: 'mercedem' should read 'mercede', as the construction with 'designata' requires; translated accordingly.

items.text: Quod caput est , sit principi persuasum totius reipublicæ majorem quam ipsius unius auctoritatem esse ; neque pessimis hominibus credat diversum affirmantibus gratificandi studio ; quæ magna pernicies est.
items.translation: Above all, let the prince be persuaded that the authority of the whole commonwealth is greater than his own alone, and let him not believe the worst of men who, eager to please him, assert the contrary; that is a great bane.

items.text: Ne cogatur tantum sciens aut imprudens sibi conscire mortem : quod esse nefas judicamus veneno in potu aut cibo quod hauriat qui perimendus est , aut simili alia re temperato.
items.translation: Only let him not be forced, knowingly or unknowingly, to bring about his own death; which we judge to be wrong when poison is mixed into the drink or food that the man to be killed is to consume, or into some other similar thing.
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.7

items.text: miseram pacem , vel bello bene mutari
items.translation: a wretched peace is well exchanged even for war

items.text: Dissimulandum censeo quatenus salus publica patiatur , privatimque corruptis moribus princeps contingat ; alioquin si rempublicam in periculum vocat , si patriæ religionis contemptor existit , neque medicinam ullam recipit , abdicandum judico alium substituendum : quod in Hispania non semel fuisse factum scimus ; quasi fera irritata omnium telis peti debet , cum humanitate abdicata tyrannum induat. Sic Petro rege ob immanitatem dejecto publice , Henricus ejus frater , quamvis ex impari matre regnum obtinuit. Sic Henrico , hujus ab nepote ob ignaviam pravosque mores abdicato procerum suffragiis , primum Alfonsus ejus frater , recte an secus non disputo , sed tamen in tenera ætate rex est proclamatus : deinde defuncto Alfonso , Elisabeth , ejus soror , Henrico invito , rerum summam ad se traxit , regio tantum nomine abstinens dum ille vixit.
items.translation: I think it should be borne so far as the public welfare allows, if the prince is corrupt only in his private morals; otherwise, if he brings the commonwealth into danger, if he shows himself a despiser of his country's religion and accepts no remedy, I judge that he should be deposed and another put in his place: which we know has been done more than once in Spain. Like an enraged wild beast he must be attacked with everyone's weapons, since, having cast off humanity, he puts on the tyrant. Thus, when King Peter was publicly deposed for his cruelty, Henry his brother, though born of a mother of unequal rank, obtained the kingdom. Thus, when Henry, his great-great-grandson, was deposed by the votes of the nobles for his sloth and depraved morals, first Alfonso his brother (whether rightly or wrongly I do not dispute) was nevertheless proclaimed king at a tender age; then, on Alfonso's death, his sister Elisabeth (Isabella), against Henry's will, took the supreme power to herself, abstaining only from the royal title while he lived.
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.3
items.note: 'ab nepote' is printed for 'abnepote', great-great-grandson.

items.text: A quibus malis innumeris , ipso juvante qui post vulnera medetur & sanat , liberati sumus per serenissimum principem regem & dominum nostrum , Dominum ROBERTUM , qui pro populo & hæreditate suis de manibus inimicorum liberandis , quasi alter Maccabæus aut Josue labores & tædia , inedias & pericula læto sustinuit animo. Quem etiam divina dispositio & juxta leges & consuetudines nostras , quas usque ad mortem sustinere volumus , juris successio & debitus nostrorum consensus & assensus nostrum fecerunt principem atque regem. Cui tanquam illi per quem salus in populo facta est , pro nostra libertate tuenda , tam jure quam meritis tenemur , & volumus in omnibus adhærere. Quem si ab inceptis desistet
items.translation: From these countless evils, with the help of Him who after wounding heals and makes whole, we have been set free by our most serene prince, king and lord, the Lord Robert, who, to deliver his people and his heritage from the hands of their enemies, bore toil and weariness, hunger and danger with a cheerful spirit, like another Maccabaeus or Joshua. Him, too, divine providence and, according to our laws and customs, which we will uphold unto death, the succession of right and the due consent and assent of our people have made our prince and king. To him, as to the one through whom salvation has been wrought for the people, we are bound, both by right and by his merits, for the defence of our liberty, and we are resolved to adhere to him in all things. But if he should abandon what he has begun,
items.source: Declaration of Arbroath (letter of the Scottish barons to the Pope, 6 April 1320)
items.note: The sentence breaks off here and continues in the next part of the note.

items.text: regi Anglorum , aut Anglicis nos , aut regnum nostrum volens subjicere tanquam inimicum nostrum , & sui nostrique juris subversorem statim expellere niteremur , & alium regem nostrum , qui ad deffensionem nostram sufficiet faciemus. Quia quamdiu centum viri remanserint , nunquam Anglorum dominio aliquatenus volumus subjugari. Non enim propter gloriam , divitias , aut honores pugnamus , sed propter libertatem solummodo , quam nemo bonus nisi simul cum vita amittit.
items.translation: [But if he should abandon what he has begun,] wishing to subject us or our kingdom to the king of the English or to the English, we would at once strive to drive him out as our enemy and the subverter of his own right and ours, and we will make another our king who will be able to defend us. For as long as a hundred men remain alive, we will never on any terms be brought under the dominion of the English. For we fight not for glory, riches or honours, but for liberty alone, which no good man gives up except with his life.
items.source: Declaration of Arbroath (letter of the Scottish barons to the Pope, 6 April 1320)

items.text: Populi patroni non pauciora neque minora præsidia habent. Certe a republica unde ortum habet regia potestas , rebus exigentibus , regens in jus vocari posse , & si sanitatem respuat , principatu spoliari ; neque ita in principem jura potestatis transtulit , ut non sibi majorem reservarit potestatem.
items.translation: The champions of the people have no fewer and no lesser defences. Certainly [they say] the ruler can, when circumstances require, be summoned to judgment by the commonwealth, from which royal power takes its origin, and, if he refuses a cure, be stripped of his rule; nor did the commonwealth transfer the rights of power to the prince in such a way as not to reserve a greater power to itself.
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.6
items.note: The infinitives 'vocari posse' and 'spoliari' depend on an unexpressed verb of saying, supplied as '[they say]'.

items.text: Est tamen salutaris cogitatio , ut sit principibus persuasum , si rempublicam opprefserint. Si vitiis & fœditate intolerandi erunt , ea conditione vivere ut non jure tantum sed cum laude & gloria perimi possint.
items.translation: Yet it is a salutary thought that princes should be persuaded that, if they oppress the commonwealth, if they become intolerable through their vices and vileness, they live on such terms that they may be put to death not only lawfully but with praise and glory.
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.6
items.note: 'opprefserint' is a misprint for 'oppresserint', and the full stop after it splits a single sentence.

items.text: Nimirum, quod publicæ salutis causa & communi consensu statutum est, eadem multitudinis voluntate, rebus exigentibus immutari quid obstat ?
items.translation: Surely, what prevents something established for the sake of the public welfare and by common consent from being changed by the same will of the multitude when circumstances require?
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.4

items.text: Nescio quomodo nihil tam absurde dici potest, quod non dicatur ab aliquo philosophorum.
items.translation: Somehow or other, nothing can be said so absurd that it is not said by one of the philosophers.

items.text: Forma divortii matrimonialis inter Johannem filium regis Bohemiæ & Margaretham Ducissam Karinthiæ
items.translation: Form of the matrimonial divorce between John, son of the King of Bohemia, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia
items.source: Act of Emperor Louis IV (1341), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, p. 154

items.text: per auctoritatem
items.translation: by the authority
items.source: Act of Emperor Louis IV (1341), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, p. 154
items.note: The phrase continues after 'dit-il' with 'nobis rite debitam & concessam'.

items.text: nobis rite debitam & concessam
items.translation: duly owed and granted to us
items.source: Act of Emperor Louis IV (1341), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, p. 154
items.note: Completes 'per auctoritatem': 'by the authority duly owed and granted to us'.

items.text: Forma dispensationis super affinitate consanguinitatis inter Ludovicum Marchionem Brandenburg , & Margaretham Ducissam Karinthiæ , nec non legitimatio liberorum procreandorum, factæ per Dom. Ludovic. IV. Rom. Imper.
items.translation: Form of the dispensation concerning the blood relationship between Louis, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Margaret, Duchess of Carinthia, together with the legitimation of the children to be born to them, granted by the Lord Louis IV, Emperor of the Romans
items.source: Act of Emperor Louis IV (1341), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, p. 156
items.note: 'affinitate consanguinitatis' (literally 'affinity of consanguinity') is rendered as 'blood relationship'.

items.text: infra gradus affinitatis sanguinis præsertim infra fratres & sorores. De cujus legis præceptis dispensare solummodo pertinet ad auctoritatem imperatoris seu principis Romanorum
items.translation: within the degrees of blood relationship, especially among brothers and sisters. To dispense from the precepts of this law belongs solely to the authority of the emperor or prince of the Romans.
items.source: Act of Emperor Louis IV (1341), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, p. 156
items.note: 'infra' is used in the medieval sense of 'within, among'.

items.text: Nam , ut verè loquamur , superstitio fusa per gentes , oppressit omnium sere animos , atque hominum imbecillitatem occupavit... , multum enim & nobismet ipsis , & nostris profuturi videbamur , si eam funditus sustulissemus. Non vero ( id enim diligenter intelligi volo ) superstitione tollendâ religio tollitur. Nam & majorum instituta tueri sacris , cæremoniisque retinendis , sapientis est : & esse præstantem aliquam æternamque naturam , & eam suspiciendam , admirandamque hominum generi , pulchritudo mundi ordoque rerum cœlestium cogit confiteri
items.translation: For, to speak truly, superstition, spread throughout the nations, has overwhelmed almost everyone's mind and taken hold of human weakness... for we thought we would do a great service both to ourselves and to our fellow citizens if we had rooted it out entirely. Yet (and I want this to be carefully understood) religion is not abolished by abolishing superstition. For it is the part of a wise man to uphold the institutions of our ancestors by keeping up their sacred rites and ceremonies; and the beauty of the world and the order of the heavenly bodies compel us to acknowledge that there exists some excellent and eternal nature, and that it ought to be looked up to and admired by the human race.
items.note: 'sere' is a misprint for 'fere' (almost).

items.text: Harum ego religionum nullam unquam contemnendam putavi : mihique ita persuasi , Romulum auspiciis , Numam sacris constitutis fundamenta jecisse nostræ civitatis : quæ nunquam profecto sine summa placatione Deorum immortalium tanta esset potuisset. Habes , Balbe , quid Cotta , quid pontifex sentiat. Fac nunc ergo intelligam , quid tu sentias : a te enim philosopho rationem accipere debeo religionis ; majoribus autem nostris , etiam nulla ratione reddita , credere
items.translation: Of these religious observances I have never thought that any should be despised, and I have persuaded myself that Romulus by the auspices and Numa by instituting the sacred rites laid the foundations of our state, which surely could never have become so great without the utmost appeasement of the immortal gods. There you have, Balbus, what Cotta thinks and what the pontiff thinks. Now, then, let me understand what you think: for from you, a philosopher, I ought to receive a reasoned account of religion, whereas our ancestors I ought to believe even when no reason is given.
items.note: 'tanta esset potuisset' is a misprint for 'tanta esse potuisset' ('could have become so great').

items.text: Deorum injuriæ Diis curæ
items.translation: Wrongs done to the gods are the gods' concern.

items.text: Qui secus faxit, Deus ipse vindex erit.... Qui non paruerit, capitale esto
items.translation: Whoever does otherwise, God himself will be the avenger.... Whoever does not obey, let it be a capital offence.
items.note: 'faxit' is an archaic form of 'fecerit', in the style of the old laws Cicero imitates.

items.text: Quas ( religiones ) non metu ,sed ea conjunctione, quæ est homini cum Deo , conservandas puto
items.translation: Which (religious observances) I think should be preserved not out of fear, but because of the bond that exists between man and God.
items.note: '( religiones )' is an insertion by Vattel, supplying the antecedent of 'Quas'.

items.text: tantum religio potuit suadere malorum
items.translation: so great the evils that religion could prompt!

items.text: scire te volumus , quod in spiritualibus & temporalibus nobis subes
items.translation: We want you to know that you are subject to us in spiritual and temporal matters.
items.source: Boniface VIII, letter to Philip IV of France

items.text: Agite nunc , quæso , patres & principes sanctissimi , ut omnis mundus intelligat & cognoscat , quia si potestis in cœlo ligare & solvere, potestis in terra imperia , regna , principatus , ducatus , marchias , comitatus & omnium hominum possessiones pro meritis tollere unicuique & concedere
items.translation: Act now, I beg you, most holy fathers and princes, so that the whole world may understand and know that, if you can bind and loose in heaven, you can on earth take away from each man and grant to each, according to his deserts, empires, kingdoms, principalities, duchies, marches, counties and the possessions of all men.
items.source: Gregory VII, speech to the council at Rome

items.text: Imperium non præest sacerdotio sed subest & ei obedire tenetur
items.translation: The empire does not stand above the priesthood but beneath it, and is bound to obey it.
items.source: Canon law, rubric of cap. VI, De majoritate et obedientia

items.text: Et est multum allegable
items.translation: And it is well worth citing.
items.source: Author of the rubric, cap. VI, De majoritate et obedientia
items.note: 'allegable' is late legal Latin for 'fit to be alleged', i.e. cited in argument.

items.text: Tantum sacerdos prastat regi , quantum homo bestiâ
items.translation: A priest surpasses a king as much as a man surpasses a beast.
items.note: 'prastat' is a misprint for 'præstat' (surpasses).

items.text: Cognitio causæ contra ecclesiasticos , etiam pro delicto læsæ majestatis fieri debet a judice ecclesiastico
items.translation: Cognizance of a case against ecclesiastics, even for the crime of lèse-majesté, must be taken by an ecclesiastical judge.
items.source: Congregation of Immunity, in Ricci, Synopsis decretorum, p. 105

items.text: Indecorum est laicos homines viros ecclesiasticos judicare
items.translation: It is unseemly for laymen to judge men of the Church.
items.source: Canon law, Decretum C. XVI q. 7 c. 22

items.text: omnia ecclesiarum jura tollere
items.translation: to take away all the rights of the churches
items.source: French prelates to Philip VI (1329), in Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus, Dipl. LXVII

items.text: Imperatoriam majestatem non solum armis decoratam , sed etiam legibus oportet esse armatam : ut utrumque tempus , & bellorum , & pacis , recte possit gubernari
items.translation: Imperial majesty ought not only to be adorned with arms but also armed with laws, so that both times, of war and of peace, may be rightly governed.

items.text: alma libertas
items.translation: nurturing liberty
items.note: "Alma" (nourishing, kindly) is the epithet the Romans gave to things that sustain life, such as the earth or a mother.

items.text: videtur esse matrimonii & stupri differentia, sed utrobique est communicatio. Ergo , inquis , & primas nuptias damnas ? Nec immerito , quoniam & ipsa constant ex eo quod est stuprum.
items.translation: There seems to be a difference between marriage and fornication, but in both there is intercourse. "So," you say, "do you condemn even first marriages?" Not without reason, since they too consist of that which is fornication.
items.note: "First marriages" means a first (single) marriage, as against the remarriage Tertullian is attacking.

items.text: Hanc tantum esse differentiam inter uxorem & scortum , quod tolerabilius sit uni esse prostitutam quam plurimis.
items.translation: [He said] that the only difference between a wife and a harlot is that it is more tolerable to be prostituted to one man than to many.

items.text: Itaque populum Campanum , urbemque Capuam , agros , delubra Deum , divina humanaque omnia , in vestram , patres conscripti , populique Romani ditionem dedimus.
items.translation: Therefore we surrender into your power, Conscript Fathers, and into that of the Roman people, the Campanian people and the city of Capua, its lands, the shrines of the gods, all things divine and human.

items.text: Motu proprio
items.translation: Of our own motion
items.source: Alexander VI, bull of 4 May 1493 (Inter caetera), from Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus no. 203
items.note: The standard formula of a papal act issued on the pope's own initiative rather than at anyone's request.

items.text: non ad vestram , vel alterius pro vobis super hoc nobis oblatæ petitionis instantiam , sed de nostra mera liberalitate , & ex certa scientia , ac de apostolicæ potestatis plenitudine , omnes insulas & terras firmas , inventas & inveniendas , detectas & detegendas versus occidentem & meridiem
items.translation: not at the instance of any petition offered to us on this matter by you or by anyone else on your behalf, but out of our own pure liberality, from certain knowledge, and from the fullness of apostolic power, all the islands and mainlands, found and to be found, discovered and to be discovered, towards the west and south
items.source: Alexander VI, bull of 4 May 1493 (Inter caetera), from Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus no. 203
items.note: These lands are the object of "we give, grant and assign" in the Latin that follows the French parenthesis.

items.text: auctoritate omnipotentis Dei , nobis in beato Petro concessa , ac vicariatus Jesu Christi , qua fungimur in terris , cum omnibus illarum dominiis , civitatibus , &c. vobis hæredibusque & successoribus vestris Castellæ & Legionis regibus in perpetuum tenore præsentium donamus , concedimus , assignamus , vosque & hæredes ac successores præfatos illorum dominos , cum plena , libera & omnimoda potestate , auctoritate & jurisdictione facimus , constituimus & deputamus.
items.translation: by the authority of almighty God granted to us in blessed Peter, and of the vicarship of Jesus Christ which we exercise on earth, [those lands,] with all their lordships, cities, etc., we by the tenor of these presents give, grant and assign in perpetuity to you and your heirs and successors, kings of Castile and León; and we make, constitute and depute you and your aforesaid heirs and successors lords of them, with full, free and complete power, authority and jurisdiction.
items.source: Alexander VI, bull of 4 May 1493 (Inter caetera), from Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus no. 203

items.text: ac quibuscunque personis , cujuscunque dignitatis , etiam imperialis & regalis , status , gradus , ordinis , vel conditionis , sub excommunicationis latæ sententiæ pœna , quam eo ipso , si contra fecerint , incurrant , districtiùs inhibemus ne ad insulas & terras firmas inventas & inveniendas , detectas & detegendas , versus occidentem & meridiem . . . . . pro mercibus habendis
items.translation: and we strictly forbid all persons whatsoever, of whatever dignity, even imperial and royal, and of whatever estate, degree, order or condition, under pain of excommunication latae sententiae, which they incur by that very act if they do the contrary, [to presume to go] to the islands and mainlands, found and to be found, discovered and to be discovered, towards the west and south . . . for the sake of trade
items.source: Alexander VI, bull of 4 May 1493 (Inter caetera), from Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus no. 203
items.note: The sentence runs on into the continuation of the note ("vel quavis alia de causa, accedere præsumant ..."); excommunication "latae sententiae" is incurred automatically, without any judge's sentence.

items.text: vel quavis alia de causa , accedere præsumant , absque vestra , ac hæredum & successorum vestrorum prædictorum licentia speciali , &c. Datum Romæ apud S. Petrum anno 1493. IV. Nonas Maii , Pontific. nostri anno 1°.
items.translation: [for the sake of trade] or for any other reason, [that they] presume to go there without the special licence of you and of your aforesaid heirs and successors, etc. Given at Rome, at St Peter's, in the year 1493, on the fourth day before the Nones of May [4 May], in the first year of our pontificate.
items.source: Alexander VI, bull of 4 May 1493 (Inter caetera), from Leibniz, Codex juris gentium diplomaticus no. 203
items.note: Completes the sentence begun in the first part of the note ("ac quibuscunque personis ... pro mercibus habendis").

items.text: Concham, urbem in Celtiberis
items.translation: Cuenca, a city among the Celtiberians
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.8
items.note: Concha is the Latin name of Cuenca in Castile.

items.text: Laræ comes
items.translation: Count of Lara
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.8
items.note: The Latin supplies the name left blank in the French "comte de..".

items.text: contractaque nobilium manu ex conventu discedit, armis tueri paratus, partam armis & virtute à majoribus immunitatem : neque passurum affirmans nobilitatis opprimendæ atque novis vectigalibus vexandæ ab eo aditu initium fieri. Mauros opprimere non esse tanti, ut graviori servitute rempublicam implicari sinant. Rex, periculo permotus, ab ea cogitatione desistit. Petrum nobiles consilio communicato quotannis convivio accipere decreverunt, ipsum & posteros navatæ operæ mercedem, rei gestæ bonæ posteritati monumentum, documentumque ne quavis occasione jus libertatis imminui patiantur.
items.translation: and, gathering a band of nobles, he left the assembly, ready to defend by arms the immunity won by the arms and valour of their ancestors, declaring that he would not allow that to be the opening through which a beginning was made of oppressing the nobility and harassing it with new taxes: crushing the Moors was not worth so much that they should let the commonwealth be entangled in a heavier servitude. The king, alarmed by the danger, gave up that plan. The nobles, having taken counsel together, decreed that Pedro and his descendants should be entertained at a banquet every year, as a reward for the service he had rendered, a memorial of the good deed for posterity, and a lesson that they should not let the right of liberty be diminished on any occasion whatever.
items.source: Mariana, De rege et regis institutione I.8

items.text: Quod domania regnorum inalienabilia & semper revocabilia dicuntur, id respectu privatorum intelligitur ; nam contra alias gentes divino privilegio opus foret.
items.translation: That the domains of kingdoms are said to be inalienable and always revocable is to be understood with respect to private persons; for against other nations a divine privilege would be needed.
items.source: Leibniz, preface to the Codex juris gentium diplomaticus

items.text: Nihil est quod adhuc de Republica putem dictum, & quo possim longius progredi, nisi sit confirmatum, non modo falsum esse illud, sine injuria non posse, sed hoc verißimum, sine summa justicia rempublicam regi non posse.
items.translation: There is nothing that I can consider so far said about the commonwealth, nor any ground from which I can go further, unless it is established not only that the saying "it cannot be governed without injustice" is false, but that this is most true: a commonwealth cannot be governed without the highest justice.
items.note: "verißimum" prints ß for ss (verissimum), and "justicia" stands for justitia.

items.text: summa justitia
items.translation: the highest justice

items.text: magis est secundum naturam, pro omnibus gentibus, si fieri possit, conservandis aut juvandis, maximos labores molestiasque suscipere, imitantem Herculem illum, quem hominum fama, beneficiorum memor, concilium cœlestium collocavit, quam vivere in solitudine, non modo sine ullis molestiis, sed etiam in maximis voluptatibus, abundantem omnibus copiis, ut excellas etiam pulchritudine & viribus. Quocirca optimo quisque & splendidissimo ingenio longe illam vitam huic anteponit.
items.translation: it is more in accordance with nature to undertake the greatest labours and troubles for the sake of preserving or helping all nations, if it can be done, imitating the famous Hercules, whom the report of men, mindful of his benefits, has placed in the council of the gods, than to live in solitude, not only free of all troubles but even amid the greatest pleasures, abounding in every resource, even supposing you also excelled in beauty and strength. Therefore every man of the best and most splendid character far prefers the former life to the latter.
items.note: Cicero's text reads "in concilio caelestium"; the edition omits "in", but the sense is the same.

items.text: qui autem civium rationem dicunt habendam, externorum negant, hi dirimunt communem humani generis societatem ; qua sublata, beneficientia, liberalitas, bonitas, justitia funditus tollitur : quæ qui tollunt, etiam adversus Deos immortales impii judicandi sunt, ab iis enim constitutam inter homines societatem evertunt.
items.translation: But those who say that regard must be had for fellow citizens but deny it to foreigners tear apart the common society of the human race; and once that is removed, beneficence, liberality, kindness and justice are utterly destroyed. Those who destroy these must be judged impious even towards the immortal gods, for they overturn the society the gods established among men.
items.note: "beneficientia" is a misprint for beneficentia.

items.text: Ergo unum debet esse omnibus propositum, ut eadem sit utilitas uniuscujusque & universorum : quam si ad se quisque rapiat, dissolvetur omnis humana consociatio. Atque si etiam hoc natura præscribit, ut homo homini, quicunque sit, ob eam ipsam
items.translation: Therefore all should have this one aim, that the advantage of each individual and of all together be the same; if anyone seizes it for himself, all human fellowship will be dissolved. And if nature also prescribes this, that a man should wish the interests of another man, whoever he may be, to be looked after for that very [reason] ...
items.note: The sentence runs on into the continuation of the note ("causam, quod is homo sit ...").

items.text: causam, quod is homo sit, consultum velit, necesse est secundum eandem naturam omnium utilitatem esse communem.
items.translation: [for that very] reason, that he is a man, then it necessarily follows, according to that same nature, that the advantage of all is common.
items.note: Completes the sentence begun in the first part of the note ("Ergo unum debet esse ...").

items.text: Olivarius dominus protector Angliæ, Scotiæ & Hiberniæ, Ludovico XIV, Francorum regi. Christianissime rex.
items.translation: Oliver, Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland, to Louis XIV, King of the French. Most Christian King.

items.text: In aula nostra alba, vester bonus amicus.
items.translation: In our White Hall, your good friend.
items.note: "Aula alba" is the Latin for Whitehall, the palace in London from which Cromwell wrote.

items.text: in judicio contradictorio
items.translation: in contested proceedings
items.note: A judgment given after both parties have appeared and been heard, as opposed to one given by default.

items.text: Sicut cælum diis, ita terras generi mortalium datas : quæque vacuæ , eas publicas esse.
items.translation: As heaven had been given to the gods, so the earth had been given to the human race; and lands that were empty were common to all.

items.text: nequeverum esse , qui suos fines tueri non potuerint , alienos occupare
items.translation: and that it was not right for those who had been unable to defend their own territory to seize that of others.
items.note: "nequeverum" is printed as one word for "neque verum".

items.text: de lucro captando , & de damno vitando
items.translation: of gain to be made, and of loss to be avoided
items.note: Shorthand for the rule that one who seeks only to avoid a loss is favoured over one who seeks to make a gain.

items.text: postquam deditionis, quàm societatis, fides sanctior erat
items.translation: since the faith owed to a surrender was more sacred than that owed to an alliance
items.note: "Postquam" has a causal sense here ("since"), not a temporal one ("after").

items.text: summum jus, summa injuria
items.translation: the highest right is the highest wrong
items.note: A proverbial maxim: to press one's right to the utmost can be the greatest injustice.

items.text: Romulidæ Cannas, ego Varnam clade notavi. Discite, mortales, non temerare fidem. Me nisi pontifices jussissent rumpere fœdus, Non ferret Scythicum Pannoniis ora jugum.
items.translation: The sons of Romulus marked Cannae with disaster; I marked Varna. Learn, mortals, not to violate good faith. Had the pontiffs not ordered me to break the treaty, the Pannonian land would not bear the Scythian yoke.
items.source: Epitaph of Uladislas, king of Poland and Hungary
items.note: "Scythian" stands for Turkish and "Pannonian" for Hungarian; the metre requires "Pannonis ora" (the Pannonian land) for the printed "Pannoniis ora".

items.text: At quid interest inter perjurum & mendacem. Qui mentiri solet , pejerare consuevit. Quem ego ut mentiatur , inducere possum , ut pejeret , exorare facile potero; nam qui semel à veritate deflexit , hic non majore religione ad perjurium quam ad mendacium perduci consuevit. Quis enim deprecatione deorum , non conscientiæ fide commovetur ? Propterea quæ pœna ab diis immortalibus perjuro , hæc eadem mendaci constituta est. Non enim ex pactione verborum quibus jusjurandum comprehenditur , sed ex perfidia & malitia , per quam insidiæ tenduntur alicui , dii immortales hominibus irasci & succensere consuerunt.
items.translation: But what difference is there between a perjurer and a liar? He who is used to lying is used to perjuring himself. A man whom I can induce to lie I shall easily be able to talk into perjuring himself; for he who has once turned aside from the truth is usually led into perjury with no greater scruple than into a lie. For who is moved by an appeal to the gods who is not moved by good faith and conscience? Therefore the same punishment that the immortal gods have appointed for the perjurer has been appointed for the liar. For it is not because of the form of words in which an oath is framed, but because of the treachery and malice by which snares are laid for someone, that the immortal gods are wont to be angry and incensed with men.

items.text: Non nostrum inter vos tantas componere lites.
items.translation: It is not for us to settle such great disputes between you.

items.text: Jura negat sibi nata , nil non arrogat armis.
items.translation: He denies that laws were made for him; there is nothing he does not claim by force of arms.

items.text: Et Romani pignus pacis ex fœdere restituerunt.
items.translation: And the Romans, in keeping with the treaty, gave back the pledge of peace.

items.text: Standum omnino est iis quæ verbis expressis, quorum manifestus est significatus, indicata fuerunt nisi omnem a negotiis humanis certitudinem removere volueris.
items.translation: One must abide entirely by what has been indicated in express words whose meaning is plain, unless you wish to remove all certainty from human dealings.

items.text: pactionem obscuram iis nocere, in quorum fuit potestate legem apertius conscribere
items.translation: that an obscure agreement harms those who had it in their power to draw up its terms more clearly.
items.note: Lex here means the clause or condition of the agreement, not a statute.

items.text: Labeo scripsit obscuritatem pacti nocere potius debere venditori, qui id dixerit, quam emptori; quia potuit re integra apertius dicere.
items.translation: Labeo wrote that the obscurity of an agreement ought to harm the seller, who stated it, rather than the buyer, because the seller could have spoken more clearly while the matter was still open.

items.text: Fraus enim adstringit, non dissolvit perjurium.
items.translation: For fraud binds the perjury tighter; it does not undo it.

items.text: incivile est, nisi tota lege perspecta, una aliqua particula ejus proposita, judicare, vel respondere
items.translation: It is improper to give judgment or a legal opinion on the strength of some single part of a law put forward, without having examined the law as a whole.

items.text: Quid ? verbis satis hoc cautum erat ? Minime. Quæ res igitur valuit ? Voluntas : quæ si, tacitis nobis, intelligi posset, verbis omnino non uteremur. Quia non potest, verba reperta sunt, non quæ impedirent, sed quæ indicarent voluntatem.
items.translation: What then? Had this been sufficiently provided for in words? Not at all. What, then, prevailed? The intention: if it could be understood while we stayed silent, we would not use words at all. Because it cannot, words were devised, not to hinder the intention but to make it known.

items.text: conventio omnis intellig itur rebus sic stantibus
items.translation: every agreement is understood as made with things remaining as they are.
items.note: 'intellig itur' is a printing break for 'intelligitur' (is understood).

items.text: Incommoda vitantis melior , quam commoda petentis est causa.
items.translation: The case of one who seeks to avoid a loss is better than that of one who seeks a gain.

items.text: beneficium imperatoris , quam plenissime interpretari debemus
items.translation: we ought to interpret the emperor's benefaction as fully as possible

items.text: quod a divina ejus indulgentia proficiscatur
items.translation: because it proceeds from his divine generosity

items.text: deinde utra lex iubeat , utra vetet. Nam sæpe ea , quæ vetat , quasi exceptione quadam corrigere videtur illam quæ jubet.
items.translation: Next, which law commands and which forbids. For often the law that forbids seems to correct the one that commands, as if by a kind of exception.

items.text: Primum igitur leges oportet contendere , considerando utra lex ad majores , hoc est , ad utiliores , ad honestiores , ac magis necessarias res pertineat. Ex quo conficitur , ut si leges duæ , aut si plures , aut quotquot erunt , conservari non possint , quia discrepent inter se , ea maxime conservanda putetur , quæ ad maximas res pertinere videatur.
items.translation: First, then, the laws must be compared, by considering which of them concerns the greater matters, that is, the more useful, the more honourable and the more necessary. From this it follows that if two laws, or more, or however many there may be, cannot all be kept because they conflict with one another, that one should be held most worth keeping which appears to concern the greatest matters.

items.text: nam maxime conservanda est ea (lex) , quæ diligentissima , & sancta est ( vel potius ,) quæ diligentissime sancta est.
items.translation: for that (law) is most to be kept which is most careful, and sanctioned (or rather) which is most carefully sanctioned.
items.note: Vattel's '(vel potius)', 'or rather', corrects the reading 'diligentissima, & sancta' to Cicero's 'diligentissime sancta', where 'sancta' means guarded by a penalty.

items.text: Parcere subjectis , & debellare superbos.
items.translation: To spare those who submit, and to subdue the proud.

items.text: Una salus . . . nullam sperare salutem.
items.translation: The one safety . . . is to hope for no safety.
items.note: The dots stand for a word Vattel leaves out of the line, 'victis' ('for the vanquished').

items.text: Nam, ut Plato ait, nemo prudens punit quia peccatum est, sed ne peccetur.
items.translation: For, as Plato says, no sensible man punishes because a wrong has been done, but so that no wrong may be done.

items.text: ex pacto vel fœdere
items.translation: by agreement or treaty

items.text: omnia quæ defendi , repetique & ulcisci fás sit
items.translation: all the things that it is right to defend, to reclaim and to avenge

items.text: justum est bellum, quibus necessarium, & pia arma, quibus nulla nisi in armis relinquitur spes
items.translation: war is just for those to whom it is necessary, and arms are holy for those who are left no hope except in arms

items.text: casus fœderis
items.translation: the case of the alliance
items.note: Vattel's term, defined in §88 as the circumstances in which the treaty of alliance obliges the ally to act.

items.text: ex pacto vel fœdere
items.translation: by agreement or treaty

items.text: Neque se in obsides innoxios, sed in ipsos, si defecerint, sæviturum : nec ab inermi, sed ab armato hoste, pœnas expetiturum.
items.translation: [He said] that he would vent his anger not on innocent hostages but on themselves, if they revolted, and would exact punishment not from an unarmed enemy but from an armed one.
items.note: The Latin is in indirect speech, governed by a verb of saying in Livy's text.

items.text: Nec Antigonum, nec quemquam ducum, sic velle vincere, ut ipse in se exemplum pessimum statuat.
items.translation: That neither Antigonus nor any of the generals would wish to win in such a way as to set the worst of precedents against himself.

items.text: Quem quidem [ Bessum ] cruci adsixum videre festino, omnibus regibus, gentibusque fidei, quam violavit, meritas pœnas solventem.
items.translation: Him [Bessus] I am eager to see nailed to the cross, paying to all kings and nations the penalty he deserves for the good faith he has violated.
items.note: 'adsixum' is a misprint for 'adfixum' (fastened); '[ Bessum ]' is the editor's insertion.

items.text: Οὐδὲ γὰρ ταῦτα τῇ χάριτι μηνύομεν, ἀλλ' ὅπως μὴ τὸ ἴσον πάθος ἡμῖν διαβολὴν ἐνέγκῃ
items.translation: For we do not disclose this to win your favour, but so that the like misfortune may not bring reproach upon us.
items.note: τὸ ἴσον πάθος ('the like misfortune') is probably a misreading of Plutarch's τὸ σὸν πάθος ('your misfortune'); translated as printed.

items.text: Sed communis exempli & fidei ergo visum est, uti te salvum velimus ; ut esset, quem armis vincere possemus.
items.translation: But for the sake of the common example and of good faith we have decided that we want you safe, so that there may be someone whom we can defeat in arms.

items.text: Armis bellà, non venenis, geri debere.
items.translation: That wars ought to be waged with arms, not with poisons.
items.note: 'bellà' is a misprint for 'bella' (wars).

items.text: Non fraude, neque occultis, sed palàm & armatum populum Romanum hostes suos ulcisci.
items.translation: That the Roman people took vengeance on its enemies not by fraud nor by secret means, but openly and in arms.

items.text: De salute certatum est.
items.translation: The contest was for survival itself.

items.text: Dolus an virtus, quis in hoste requirat
items.translation: Stratagem or valour: who would ask which, in dealing with an enemy?

items.text: Ille non inclusus equo, Minerva Sacra mentito, malè feriatos Troas, & lætam Priami choreis Falleret aulam : Sed palam captis gravis
items.translation: He [Achilles] would not have shut himself in the horse that falsely posed as a sacred offering to Minerva, to deceive the Trojans in their ill-timed holiday and Priam's court rejoicing in dances; but openly, terrible to the captured...
items.note: 'Minerva' is a misprint for Horace's 'Minervae' (to Minerva).

items.text: Viriati etiam cædes duplicem perfidiæ accusationem recepit : in amicis, quod eorum manibus interemptus est : in Q. Servilio Cæpione consule, quia isceleris hujus auctor, impunitate promissà, fuit ; victoriamque non meruit, sed emit.
items.translation: The killing of Viriathus also drew a double charge of treachery: against his friends, because he was slain by their hands; and against the consul Q. Servilius Caepio, because he was the instigator of this crime, having promised them impunity, and did not earn the victory but bought it.
items.note: 'isceleris' is a misprint for 'is sceleris' (he ... of this crime).

items.text: Quæ victoria, quia empta erat, à senatu non probata.
items.translation: This victory, because it had been bought, was not approved by the senate.

items.text: Transfugam jure belli recipimus.
items.translation: We receive a deserter by the law of war.

items.text: Eadem fide indicatum Pyrrho regi medicum, vitæ ejus insidiantem : eadem Faliscis vinctum traditum proditorem liberorum regis.
items.translation: With the same good faith King Pyrrhus was told of the physician plotting against his life; with the same, the man who betrayed the king's children was handed over in chains to the Faliscans.

items.text: Inter dominum & servum nulla amicitia est ; etiam in pace belli tamen jura servantur.
items.translation: Between master and slave there is no friendship; even in peace the rights of war are still kept up.

items.text: Quid , si pœnam , inquit ( consul ) , remittimus vobis , qualem nos pacem vobiscum habituros speremus ? Si bonam dederitis , inquit , & fidam , & perpetuam : si malam , haud diuturnam. Tum verò minari , nec id ambiguè Privernatem quidam , & illis vocibus ad rebellandum incitari pacatos populos. Pars melior senatûs ad meliora responsa trahere , & dicere , viri , & liberi vocem auditam : an credi posse ullum populum , aut hominem denique in ea conditione , cujus eum pœniteat , diutiùs quàm necesse sit mansurum ? Ibi pacem esse fidam , ubi voluntarii pacati sint : neque eo loco , ubi servitutem esse velint , fidem sperandam esse.
items.translation: 'What if we remit your punishment,' said the consul, 'what sort of peace may we hope to have with you?' 'If you give us a good one,' he said, 'a faithful and lasting one; if a bad one, not a long one.' Then some cried out that the Privernate was threatening, and not obscurely, and that such words were inciting peoples at peace to rebel. The better part of the senate took his answers in a more favourable sense and said that they had heard the voice of a man, and of a free man: could it be believed that any people, or indeed any man, would stay longer than he must in a condition that grieved him? Peace was faithful where men had been pacified of their own will; and where slavery was to be imposed, no good faith could be hoped for.

items.text: Certè id firmissimum longè imperium est , quo obedientes gaudent.
items.translation: Certainly by far the firmest rule is the one in which those who obey take pleasure.

items.text: dicens evenire potuisse ut essent insidiæ
items.translation: saying that it could have happened that there was an ambush
items.source: Vulcacius Gallicanus, Life of Avidius Cassius, via Grotius III.18.1

items.text: Belli commercia Turnus Sustulit ista prior
items.translation: Turnus was the first to do away with such dealings of war

items.text: Nam cum sint duo genera decertandi , unum per disceptationem , alterum per vim , cumque illud proprium sit hominis , hoc belluarum , confugiendum est ad posterius , si uti non licet superiore.
items.translation: For since there are two ways of settling a dispute, one by discussion, the other by force, and since the former is proper to man, the latter to beasts, one must resort to the latter only if one may not use the former.
items.note: The passage is at De officiis I.11.34, not in chapter 2 as the note's reference has it.

items.text: Nomen legati
items.translation: The name of envoy
items.note: Subject of the sentence that resumes after 'dit Cicéron'.

items.text: ejusmodi esse debet , quod non modo inter sociorum jura , sed etiam inter hostium tela incolume versetur
items.translation: must be such that it remains unharmed not only amid the rights of allies but even amid the weapons of enemies

items.text: legati contra jus gentium arma capiunt
items.translation: the envoys take up arms against the law of nations
items.note: The passage is at Livy V.36; the chapter number in the note's reference is doubtful.

items.text: Et quamquam visi sunt ( legati ) commisisse, ut hostium loco essent , jus tamen gentium valuit
items.translation: And although they (the envoys) seemed to have acted so as to be counted as enemies, the law of nations nevertheless prevailed.
items.note: '(legati)' is Vattel's insertion to name the subject.

items.text: Σκίπιων, ουκ, ἔφη, δεῖν πράττειν ὁ [?]οῖς Καρχηδονίοις ἐγκαλοῦσι
items.translation: Scipio said that they must not do what they reproach the Carthaginians for.
items.note: The print is damaged: 'ὁ [?]οῖς' is read as ὃ τοῖς ('what ... the'), and the accent of 'Σκίπιων' is misplaced.

items.text: Ideo enim non datur actio ( adversus legatum ) ne ab officio suscepto legationis avocetur (b), ne impediatur legatio
items.translation: For no action is granted (against an envoy) so that he may not be called away from the office of envoy he has undertaken, so that the embassy may not be hindered.
items.note: Vattel joins two Digest texts, marked (b) and (c); '(adversus legatum)' is his insertion.

items.text: Nec pontificem (in jus vocari oportet) dum sacra facit
items.translation: Nor (ought) a pontiff (to be summoned to court) while he is performing sacred rites.
items.note: The bracketed words are supplied by Vattel to complete the sentence.
